rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage introduces the worldly and afterlife qualities of God's purified servants, distinguishing them from those who turn away from worship; their genitive link to al-Rahman singles them out for mercy or privilege.
rows.anchor: بيان أوصاف خلص عباد الله تعالى وأحوالهم الدنيوية والأخروية

rows.speaker: ابن بحر
rows.claim: Most take عباد as the plural of عبد, while Ibn Bahr derives it as the plural of عابد.
rows.anchor: والاكثرون أن عبادا هنا جمع عبد وقال ابن بحر : جمع عابد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the عبد derivation, servitude means accepting what God does; on عابد, worship means doing what pleases the Lord.
rows.anchor: وهي أن يفعل ما يرضاه الرب وعلى الأول من العبودية وهي أن يرضى ما يفعله الرب

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Raghib defines servitude as displaying abasement and worship as a more complete degree, the utmost humility.
rows.anchor: العبودية إظهار التذلل والعبادة أبلغ منها لأنها غاية التذلل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another distinction makes worship obedience for reward and escape from punishment, servitude gratitude for God's favor, and عبودة obedience solely for God's command and inherent worthiness.
rows.anchor: وفوق ذلك العبودة وهو فعل وترك ما ذكر لمجرد أمره سبحانه ونهيه عز وجل واستحقاقه سبحانه الذاتي

rows.speaker: اليماني
rows.claim: The Yamani reading has ʿubbād, with ḍamma on ʿayn and a doubled bāʾ, unanimously the plural of عابد.
rows.anchor: ويوافقه قراءة اليماني ( وعباد ) بضم العين وتشديد الباء

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan reads وَعَبْد with both first letters vocalized ḍamma; al-Akhfash treats it as the plural of عبد, like سقف, with an Arabic verse cited as evidence.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن ( وعبد ) بضم العين والباء وهو كما قال الأخفش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: عباد is a subject whose predicate could be the final demonstrative-led sentence of the surah; al-Alusi prefers the nearer predicate, الذين يمشون.
rows.anchor: والثاني وهو الأقرب أنه قوله تعالى ( الذين يمشون على الأرض هونا (

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: هون means gentleness and ease; it is accusative either as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, مشيا هونا, or as a circumstantial phrase describing their walking.
rows.anchor: والهون مصدر بمعنى اللين والرفق ونصبه إا على أنه نعت لمصدر محذوف أي مشيا هونا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، مجاهد، عكرمة، الفضيل بن عياض
rows.claim: They explain the walk as measured, calm, dignified, and well-mannered, without stamping or swaggering.
rows.anchor: وروي نحو هذا عن ابن عباس ومجاهد وعكرمة والفضيل بن عياض وغيرهم

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله
rows.claim: Abu ʿAbd Allah says the praised walk follows one's natural disposition, without affectation or strutting.
rows.anchor: وعن الامام أبي عبد الله رضي الله تعالى عنه أن الهون مشي الرجل بسجيته

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: Al-Amidi relates that ʿUmar rebuked a swaggering youth, invoking this verse and telling him to walk moderately.
rows.anchor: عن عمر رضي الله تعالى عنه أنه رأى غلاما يتبختر في مشيته فقال له : إن البخترة مشية نكرة

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A report from Abu Hurayra and Ibn ʿAbbas attributes to the Prophet the saying that quick walking removes the beauty of religion.
rows.anchor: قالا قال رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم سرعة المشي تذهب بهاء الدين

rows.speaker: ميمون بن مهران
rows.claim: Ibn Abi Hatim transmits that هون means “forbearing” in Syriac, which would make it a circumstantial expression only.
rows.anchor: عن ميمون بن مهران إن ( هونا ) بمعنى حلماء بالسريانية فيكون حالا لا غير

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Raghib explains هون as self-humbling without disgrace, a praiseworthy trait, and cites the saying “the believer is gentle and kind.”
rows.anchor: وفسره الراغب بتذلل الانسان في نفسه لما لايلحق به غضاضة وهو الممدوح ومنه الحديث المؤمن هين لين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent sense is Arabic gentleness and ease, and the verse specifically praises composure and dignity in walking; gentleness in other affairs follows by habit.
rows.anchor: والظاهر بقاء المشي على حقيقته وأن المراد مدحهم بالسكينة والوقار فيه من غير تعميم

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya takes the verse to praise freedom from harshness and rudeness throughout one's dealings, since walking entails social contact.
rows.anchor: اختار ابن عطية أن المراد مدحهم بعدم الخشونة والفظاظة في سائر أمورهم وتصرفاتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi rejects as untenable the claim that only slow walking is praised: a slow, gentle walker may still be a predatory wolf.
rows.anchor: وأما أن يكون المراد مدحهم بالمشي وحده هونا فباطل فكم ماش هونا رويدا وهو ذئب أطلس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya cites the Prophet's measured gait as the model for the verse; al-Alusi notes two objections to this argument.
rows.anchor: وقد كان صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم يتكفأ في مشيته كانما يمشي في صبب وهو عليه الصلاة والسلام الصدر في هذه الآية

rows.speaker: اليماني، السلمي
rows.claim: They read يمشون in a passive, intensified form.
rows.anchor: وقرأ اليماني والسلمي ( يمشون ) مبنيا للمفعول مشددا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ignorant are fools and ill-mannered people; the cited verse line illustrates their provocation.
rows.anchor: أي السفهاء وقليلو الأدب كما في قوله : ألا لايجهلن أحد علينا فنجهل فوق جهل الجاهلينا

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh parses سلاما as an emphatic verbal noun for an implied verb, meaning “we disengage peacefully”; the ordinary greeting is excluded because the verse is Meccan.
rows.anchor: سلاما مصدر أقيم مقام التسليم وهو مصدر مؤكد لفعله المضمر والتقدير نتسلم تسلما منكم

rows.speaker: الأصم
rows.claim: Al-Asamm understands سلاما as a farewell expressing disengagement, like Abraham's farewell to his father.
rows.anchor: وقال الأصم : هو سلام توديع لاتحية كقول إبراهيم عليه السلام لأبيه

rows.speaker: مجاهد، صاحب الكشف
rows.claim: Mujahid says they utter a sound or upright statement; al-Alusi objects that the wording points to the actual word سلام, while al-Kashf reconciles this as any sin-free expression of peaceful disengagement.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد : المراد قالوا قولا سديدا

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشف
rows.claim: Al-Kashf holds that “Peace be upon you; we seek no company of the ignorant” is sound speech and that this or equivalent wording expresses peaceful, sin-free withdrawal.
rows.anchor: فان قولهم سلام عليكم من سداد القول أيضا كيف والظاهر أن خصوص اللفظ غير مقصود

rows.speaker: المأمون
rows.claim: A history cited in al-Bahr says Ibrahim ibn al-Mahdi, hostile to ʿAli, dreamed that ʿAli answered his challenge with “peace”; al-Maʾmun explained the verse as the most eloquent reply, and Ibrahim was shamed.
rows.anchor: قال : كان يقول لي : سلاما سلاما فقال المأمون : يا عم قد أجابك بأبلغ جواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse praises overlooking fools and not answering their abuse; it does not address dealings with unbelievers and therefore does not conflict with the later fighting command or become abrogated by it.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن المراد مدحهم بالاغضاء عن السفهاء وترك مقابلتهم في الكلام ولا تعرض في الآية لمعاملتهم مع الكفرة

rows.speaker: أبو العالية، عطية
rows.claim: Abu al-ʿAliya is reported, and ʿAtiyya is said to choose, that the verse was abrogated regarding unbelievers by the fighting verse.
rows.anchor: ونقل عن أبي العالية واختاره عطية أنها نسخت بالنظر إلى الكفرة بآية القتال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The فاء orders arrival at Pharaoh as a consequence of the preceding promise; going means reaching the destination, not merely setting out toward it.
rows.anchor: الفاء في قوله تعالى ( فأتيا فرعون فقولا إنا رسولا رب العالمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: رسول is singular because it is originally a verbal noun used descriptively, like رجل عدل; two cited poems by Kathir ʿAzza and al-ʿAbbas ibn Mirdas attest the singular form.
rows.anchor: وافرد الرسول هنا لأنه مصدر بحسب الأصل وصف به كما يوصف بغيره من المصادر للمبالغة كرجل عدل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other explanations for the singular include the brothers' unity, one sender, one message, or إنا meaning “our speech”; these allow one predicate for both.
rows.anchor: أو لاتحادهما للاخوة أو لوحده المرسل أو المرسل به أو لأن قوله تعالى ( إنا ) بمعنى إن كلامنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular also signals that each brother is charged to deliver the message even independently.
rows.anchor: وفائدته الاشارة إلى أن كلا منهما مأمور بتبليغ ذلك ولو منفردا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling God Lord of all worlds refutes Pharaoh's claim to divinity and subtly invites him to obey.
rows.anchor: وفي التعبير برب العالمين رد على اللعين ونقض لما كان أبرمه من ادعاء الألوهية وحمل لطيف له على امتثال الأمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One account says Moses and Aaron waited a year at Pharaoh's gate; the porter said someone claimed to be the Lord of the worlds' messenger, and Pharaoh admitted them to mock them.
rows.anchor: ويروى أنهما انطلقا إلى باب فرعون فلم يؤذن لهما سنة حتى قال البواب : إن ههنا إنسانا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second account has them arrive at night; Pharaoh is startled by the knock, hears the claim through his porter, and orders Moses admitted as a madman.
rows.anchor: وفي خبر آخر أنهما أتيا ليلا فقرع الباب ففزع فرعون وقال : من هذا الذي يضرب بابي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh's question about rearing Moses is meant as an expression of favor and boastful indebtedness.
rows.anchor: وأراد اللعين من قوله ( ألم نربك ) الخ الامتنان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In فينا, an omitted “our homes” is understood; وليد is an active-form noun used in the passive sense for someone recently born.
rows.anchor: و ( فينا ) على تقدير المضاف أي منازلنا والوليد فعيل بمعنى مفعول

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Raghib says وليد can originally refer to someone whose birth is either recent or remote, though the name drops as the person grows.
rows.anchor: على ما قال الراغب : يصح في الاصل لمن قرب عهده أو بعد

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some explain that وليد indicates recent birth through its intensive form, since birth itself does not vary in degree.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم : كان دلالته على قرب العهد من صيغة المبالغة وكون الولادة لاتفاوت فيها نفسها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One chronology has Moses live among them thirty years, spend ten years in Midian, preach to them for thirty years, then live fifty years after the drowning.
rows.anchor: قيل : لبث فيهم ثلاثين سنة ثم خرج إلى مدين وأقام به عشر سنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another chronology has Moses flee after striking the Egyptian at age twelve, shepherd for Shuʿayb ten years, then live eighteen more years after marrying his daughter, completing forty before his mission.
rows.anchor: وقيل : لبث فيهم اثنتي عشرة سنة ففر بعد أن وكز القبطي إلى مدين فأقام به عشر سنين

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: In one transmission Abu ʿAmr reads عمر with a still mīm; the preposed phrase من عمرك is circumstantial for سنين.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو في رواية ( من عمرك ) باسكان الميم والجار والمجرور في موضع الحال من ( سنين )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: فعلتها means “I did that deed”; on one analysis إذا means “then,” a temporal adverb detached from annexation and given fatḥa for ease and frequent use.
rows.anchor: قال فعلتها ( أي تلك الفعلة ( إذا ( أي إذ ذاك على ما أثره بعض المحققين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses admits the killing because he trusts God's protection, and qualifies it so it cannot impugn his prophethood.
rows.anchor: وأقر عليه السلام بالقتل لثقته بحفظ الله تعالى له وقيد الفعل بما يدفع كونه قادحا في النبوة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، ابن مسعود
rows.claim: A reading attributed to Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Masʿud gives الضالين the sense “ignorant”; Abu Hayyan says it appears to be an explanatory gloss, not a transmitted prophetic reading.
rows.anchor: كما نقله أبو حيان في البحر لكنه قال : ويظهر أن ذاك تفسير للضالين

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Al-Alusi favors Qatada's explanation: Moses acted unknowingly and without intending the killing, having meant only a disciplinary blow.
rows.anchor: وأراد عليه السلام بذلك على ماروي عن قتادة أنه فعل ذلك جاهلا به غير متعمدا إياه

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd similarly explains that Moses did not know his blow would kill the Egyptian.
rows.anchor: وفي معنى ما ذكر ما روي عن ابن زيد من أن المعنى وأنا من الجاهلين بأن وكزتي تأتي على نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view takes الضالين as people who act boldly without regard for consequences; al-Alusi says this works for one explanation of the reply.
rows.anchor: وقيل : المعنى فعلتها مقدما عليها من غير مبالاة بالعواقب على أن الجهل بمعنى الاقدام

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say الضلال means love, as in Joseph 12:95, so Moses killed the Egyptian out of zeal for God; al-Alusi dismisses this as absurd.
rows.anchor: قيل : إن الضلال ههنا المحبة كما فسر بذلك في قوله تعالى إنك لفي ضلالك القديم

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another view says Moses was ignorant of the religious law, invoking the use of ضال in 93:7; al-Alusi notes this interpretation.
rows.anchor: ومثله ما قيل أراد من الجاهلين بالشرائع وفسر الضلال بذلك في قوله تعالى ووجدك ضالا فهدى

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayda interprets الضلال as forgetfulness, as in the rule that one woman may forget and the other remind her; some apply that to forgetting the prohibition or the blow's deadly likelihood.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة : من الناسين وفسر الضلال بالنسيان في قوله تعالى أن تضل احداهما فتذكر أحداهما الأخرى

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayda, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Jurayj transmit Ibn Masʿud's reading فعلتها إذ أنا من الضالين.
rows.anchor: وأخرج أبو عبيدة وابن المنذر وابن جريج عن ابن مسعود أنه قرأ فعلتها إذ انا من الضالين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses fled when he feared harm from Pharaoh's people, after being told the council was plotting to kill him; this explains the plural “you.”
rows.anchor: ففرت ( أي خرجت هاربا ( منكم لما خفتكم ( أي حين توقعت مكروها يصيبني منكم

rows.speaker: حمزة
rows.claim: Hamza reads لما with kasra on the lām and a light mīm, construing the lām as a preposition and ما as a verbal noun: “because I feared you.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة في رواية لما بكسر اللام وتخفيف الميم على أن اللام حرف جر وما مصدرية

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi explains الحكم as prophethood; another explanation is knowledge and understanding of things as they are, with some narrowing that knowledge to what is distinctive of prophethood.
rows.anchor: فوهب لي ربي حكما ( أي نبوة أو علما وفهما للاشياء على ما هي عليه والاول مروي عن السدي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the prophethood interpretation, making Moses one of the messengers marks God's further favor of the higher rank of messengership.
rows.anchor: اشارة على ظاهر الأول من تفسيري الحكم إلى تفضله تعالى عليه برتبة هي فوق رتبة النبوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses answers that the killing preceded his mission and was unintended, since the blow was meant as discipline; he then turns back to Pharaoh's boast of raising him.
rows.anchor: من نسبة القتل إلى مسلم لكنه ليس مما أوبخ به ويقدح في نبوتي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling messengership an established divine practice magnifies its office and tells Pharaoh that Moses' mission is no novelty.
rows.anchor: وتنبيها لفرعون على أن رسالته عليه السلام ليس أمرا مبتدعا بل هو مما جرت به سنة الله تعالى شأنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: تلك points to Pharaoh's rearing of Moses; تمنها means he counts it as a favor, with the present tense evoking the scene. Another derivation from المَنّ means enumerate as a favor.
rows.anchor: وتلك ( أي التربية المفهومة من قوله : ( ألم نربك ) الخ ( نعمة تمنها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: عبد بني إسرائيل means Pharaoh subdued and enslaved them; the verb عبد الرجل means to take someone as a slave, as the cited poem illustrates.
rows.anchor: أي ذللتهم وأتخذتهم عبيدا يقال : عبدت الرجل وأعبدته إدا اتخذته عبدا قال الشاعر : علام يعبدني قومي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grammarians offer several parses for أن عبدت: a predicate of an omitted subject, circumstantial or explanatory clause, apposition to تلك or نعمة, conjunction, apposition to تمنها's pronoun, or a phrase governed by an implied preposition.
rows.anchor: وأن وما بعدها في تأويل مصدر مرفوع على أنه خبر مبتدأ محذوف والجملة حالية أو مفسرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses argues that Pharaoh's supposed favor was really a calamity: it arose from enslaving his people and intending to kill their sons; without that, Moses would not have been raised in Pharaoh's palace.
rows.anchor: نعمة ظاهرا وهي في الحقيقة نقمة حيث كانت بسبب اذلال قومي وقصدك إياهم بذبح أبنائهم

rows.speaker: الضحاك، قتادة، الأخفش، الفراء
rows.claim: Another interpretation makes the enslavement itself the “favor” Pharaoh claims, reading the clause as a repudiating question; al-Akhfash and al-Farraʾ posit an omitted interrogative hamza.
rows.anchor: قراءة الضحاك وتلك نعمة مالك أن تمنها علي وإلى ذلك ذهب قتادة وكذا الأخفش والفراء

rows.speaker: السدي، الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Suddi and al-Tabari take Moses to acknowledge Pharaoh's favor in rearing him, since Pharaoh enslaved others but spared and adopted him; al-Alusi says this is not persuasive.
rows.anchor: وإلى التأويل ذهب السدي والطبري وليس بذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse shows that an unbeliever's disbelief does not erase a favor he previously granted; the contrary view is answered by distinguishing the grounds for praise and blame.
rows.anchor: فالآية ظاهرة في أن كفر الكافر لايبطل نعمته وذهب بعضهم أن الكفر يبطل النعمة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari reads إذا in the prior verse as a conditional answer: Pharaoh accused Moses of repaying his favor with the killing, and Moses accepts that he did so.
rows.anchor: وذهب الزمخشري إلى أن إذا في قوله تعالى فعلتها إذا جواب وجزاء

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشف
rows.claim: Al-Kashf explains the conditional reading hypothetically: if the killing were ingratitude, Moses did it as repayment, but he denies it was ingratitude; “I was astray” is a second apology for acting before divine permission.
rows.anchor: وفي الكشف تحقيق ما ذكره الزمخشري أن الترتيب الذي هو معنى الشرط والجزاء حاصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Kashf's reading can accommodate وأنا من الضالين: Moses was off the right course in acting before divine permission, not in believing he owed Pharaoh repayment.
rows.anchor: وقوله : ( وأنا من الضالين ) على هذا كأنه اعتذار ثان أي كنت تستحق ذلك عندي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The most fitting way to sustain a recompense reading is to understand ضالين as bold action without concern for consequences.
rows.anchor: ولايخفى أن الأوفق بحديث الجزاء أن يكون المراد بقوله : فعلتها وأنا من الضالين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi says the conditional account is unnecessary: most interpreters make إذا simply an answer, while explaining it as a conditional reward here is strained.
rows.anchor: فان الصحيح الذي قال به الأكثرون أنها قد تتمحض للجواب وفي البحر أنهم حملوا ما في هذه الآية على ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His preferred reading treats إذا as a temporal adverb detached from annexation; if that is refused, it functions only as an answer, not as filler.
rows.anchor: والأظهر عندي معنى ما آثره بعض أفاضل المحققين من أنها ظرف مقطوع عن الاضافة

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya calls إذا a filler and then glosses it as “then”; al-Alusi says the latter works as an explanation of meaning, but not as a filler.
rows.anchor: قول ابن عطية : إنها هنا صلة في الكلام ثم قوله : وكأنها بمعنى حينئذ

rows.speaker: الطيبي
rows.claim: Al-Tibi explains the sequence: Moses delivered the ordered message, Pharaoh first challenged his upbringing and then asked about the Lord; the waw joins the questions and قال repeats because the passage is long.
rows.anchor: لما أمرهما بقوله سبحانه : ( فاتيا فرعون فقولا إنا رسول رب العالمين

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says Pharaoh first heard from his porter that a messenger claimed to represent the Lord of the worlds, then asked “what is the Lord?” on Moses' entry.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري : إن اللعين لما قال له بوابه : إن ههنا من يزعم أنه رسول رب العالمين

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشف
rows.claim: Al-Kashf defends al-Zamakhshari: the porter reported the earlier wording, while Moses spoke the later one face to face; Pharaoh first attacked Moses' character, then mocked the sender.
rows.anchor: وانتصر له صاحب الكشف فقال : أراد أنه تعالى ذكر مرة ( فقولا انا رسولا ربك

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say the encounter happened twice: first Pharaoh asked “Who is your Lord?” and later “What is the Lord of the worlds?”; Ibn ʿAbbas reports the revelation order as Taha, al-Waqiʿa, then al-Shuʿara.
rows.anchor: وجوز بعضهم وقوع الأمر مرتين وأن فرعون سأل أولا بقوله ( فمن ربكما يا موسى )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation says both times Moses and Aaron said they were messengers of the Lord of the worlds; Taha mentions God's lordship over Pharaoh because that sufficed for its purpose.
rows.anchor: وقال آخر : يحتمل أنهما إنما قالا : ( إنا رسول رب العالمين ) والاقتصار في سورة طه

rows.speaker: السكاكي
rows.claim: If the questions occurred twice, the first “Who is your Lord?” asks for an identifying attribute; al-Sakkaki instead construes it as asking the category—human, angel, or jinn—and the answer uses wise redirection.
rows.anchor: قيل : ان فرعون سأل في المرة الأولى بقوله : ( من ربكما ) طلبا للوصف المشخص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the two-question account, Pharaoh's second question asks for the essence or reality, moving to a more difficult issue for his corrupt aims.
rows.anchor: وأخرى بما رب العالمين طلبا للماهية والحقيقة انتقالا لما هو أصعب ليتوصل بذلك إلى بعض أغراضه الفاسدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ما asks about an essence whether its referent is rational or not; there is no need to replace it with من, since asking God's essence is itself unfitting.
rows.anchor: و ( ما ) يسئل بها عن الحقيقة مطلقا سواء كان المسئول عن حقيقته من أولي العلم أولا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses redirects from the unknowable essence to God's attributes by wise redirection; the difficulty of knowing the divine essence was discussed earlier.
rows.anchor: عادلا عن جوابه إلى ذكر صفاته عز وجل على نهج الاسلوب الحكيم اشارة إلى تعذر بيان الحقيقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: رب is nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject: “He is Lord of the heavens, earth, and all between them,” including elements and their derivatives.
rows.anchor: ورفع ( رب ) على أنه خبر مبتدأ محذوف أي هو رب السموات والأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “If you are certain” means certainty about anything should establish this more plainly; the observable celestial bodies are contingent because they are composite, multiple, and changing.
rows.anchor: أي إن كنتم موقنين بالأشياء محققين لها علمتم ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those contingent bodies require a necessary source; it must ground every possible thing, perceived or imperceptible, or else necessary beings multiply or some contingent things become independent.
rows.anchor: فان هذه الاجرام المحسوسة ممكنة لتركبها وتعددها وتغير أحوالها فلها مبدأ واجب لذاته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh addresses his entourage because he fears Moses' answer might lodge in their hearts.
rows.anchor: قال ( فرعون عند سماع جوابه عليه السلام خوفا من أن يعلق منه في قلوب قومه شيء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas says the entourage were five hundred nobles wearing bracelets, a privilege reserved for kings.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنهما : كانوا خمسمائة رجل عليهم الاساور وكانت للملوك خاصة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh's “Will you not listen?” expresses sarcastic astonishment and belittles Moses, implying that merely hearing the answer is enough to reject it.
rows.anchor: جوابه يريد التعجب منه والازراء بقائله وكان ذلك لعدم مطابقته للسؤال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The answer did not state God's essence as Pharaoh demanded; its proof from possibility and origination would be opaque to his ignorant people, who would not readily grasp why creation needs a necessary source.
rows.anchor: وكونه في زعمه نظرا لما عليه قومه من الجهالة غير واضح في نفسه لخفاء العلم بامكان ما ذكر أو حدوثه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses shifts to a clearer, nearer proof to fulfill his guidance role as far as possible, since the essence cannot be grasped.
rows.anchor: قال ( عدولا إلى ما هو أوضح وأقرب اعطاء لمنصب الارشاد حقه حسب الامكان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hearers' own createdness and dependence on a wise necessary being, including that of their ancestors, is more evident; self-reflection is closer and clearer than reflection on the cosmos.
rows.anchor: فان الحدوث والافتقار إلى واجب مصور حكيم في المخاطبين وآبائهم الذين ذهبوا وعدموا أظهر والنظر في الانفس أقرب وأوضح من النظر في الآفاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh calls Moses mad to turn the audience against him, portray him as failing to answer and understand, and stir their anger against his message.
rows.anchor: مبالغا في الرد والاشارة إلى عدم الاعتداد بذلك مصرحا بما ينفر قلوبهم عن قائله وقبول ما يجيء به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By saying “your messenger,” Pharaoh mocks the claim and distances himself from it; “sent to you” flatters the audience as too elevated to receive a madman's message.
rows.anchor: وسماه رسولا بطريق الاستهزاء وأضافة إلى مخاطبيه ترفعا من أن يكون مرسلا إلى نفسه

rows.speaker: مجاهد، الأعرج
rows.claim: Mujahid and al-Aʿraj read أرسل in the active voice: “the one whom his Lord sent to you.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ مجاهد والأعرج ( أرسل ) على بناء الفاعلأي الذي أرسله ربه اليكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi suggests Moses changed to the clearer second answer after Pharaoh's harsh reply and insinuation that Moses had failed to notice the first answer's obscurity to the audience.
rows.anchor: وكأنه عليه السلام لما رأى خشونة رد اللعين وإيماء منه إلا أنه عليه السلام لم يتنبه لما في جوابه الأول من الخفاء عند قومه بل كان عدوله عنه إلى الجواب الثاني
